Kussmaul breathing is deep, labored breathing seen in DKA.

rapidFireQAs.q: ADH is produced by both the supraoptic nucleus and paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus
rapidFireQAs.a: stored in posterior pituitary.

rapidFireQAs.q: If ADH is ↑, we get ↑ free water reabsorption and dilution of our serum
rapidFireQAs.a: serum sodium and osmolality ↓. Likewise, our urine becomes more concentrated, meaning urine osmolality and specific gravity ↑.

rapidFireQAs.q: If ADH is ↓, we get ↓ free water reabsorption and concentration of our serum
rapidFireQAs.a: serum sodium and osmolality ↑. Likewise, our urine becomes more dilute, meaning urine osmolality and specific gravity ↓.

rapidFireQAs.q: An increase in serum osmolality will trigger ADH release, which in turn will reabsorb more free water in the medullary collecting duct of the kidney to help re-dilute the serum back to original osmolality.
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ serum tonicity + osmolality → ↑ ADH release → dilutes serum back to normal. ↓ serum tonicity + osmolality → ↓ ADH release → concentrates serum back to normal.

rapidFireQAs.q: Estrogen causes ↑ thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) production by the liver. TBG is the protein carrier molecule for thyroid hormone in the blood. An NBME Q asks for which hormone causes the ↑ TBG in pregnancy
rapidFireQAs.a: estrogen; progesterone is wrong answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: A student might say, “Wait, but why are you giving the above bold arrows if you just gave me all sorts of transient changes in the arrows based on TBG?
rapidFireQAs.a: .” It’s because the bold arrows are what the USMLE wants. Pregnant women who are euthyroid will have normal free-T4 and increased total T4, and their TSH will be normal. The changes due to TBG rising are likely synchronous and slow enough that the patient’s TSH and free-T4 stay within reference ranges.

rapidFireQAs.q: - Q will tell you patient has SLE treated with prednisone who goes into surgery and gets a ↓↓ drop in BP to 80/40 + fluids and pressors don’t help; Q asks next best step
rapidFireQAs.a: IV hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone. What we are doing is replenishing the glucocorticoid. “Pressors” can refer to NE, E, or even desmopressin.

rapidFireQAs.q: - The Q can also tell you patient being treated with prednisone for SLE or RA experiences an acute thyroiditis (remember autoimmune diseases go together) and gets ↓↓ in BP
rapidFireQAs.a: hydrocortisone (after fluids). Or patient with autoimmune disease gets an infection + ↓↓ in BP → answer = hydrocortisone (after fluids).

rapidFireQAs.q: - ACTH is ↑ in all three types. This is the mechanism USMLE wants for the hyperplasia. That is, cortisol production is impaired in all three, so ACTH goes ↑ to compensate
rapidFireQAs.a: stimulates hyperplasia of adrenals.

rapidFireQAs.q: - The USMLE will give a vignette of CAH, followed by “which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?”
rapidFireQAs.a: “Increased ACTH secretion.” Sounds weird, but it’s on NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: - For both 21- AND 11-hydroxylase deficiencies:
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ 17-OH substrates (i.e., 17-OH-progesterone and 17-OH-pregnenolone). ↑ DHEA-S, ↑ androstenedione. If you see any of these up in the Q, you know right away answer is either 21- or 11-deficiency. This is because it’s impossible to get 17-OH substrates in 17-hydroxylase deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: - Three key details that distinguish acute diabetes mellitus from diabetes insipidus is that DM vignettes can often mention weight loss, vomiting, and/or visual changes. Weight loss is also seen in acute type II, even though the patient is usually overweight. Weight loss occurs due to ↑ catabolism. Visual changes occur due to glucose moving into the lens of the eye
rapidFireQAs.a: conversion via aldose reductase into sorbitol, which has high osmotic pull → water enters lens causing distortion.

rapidFireQAs.q: - Winter formula is used to calculate predicted pCO2 based on any change in bicarb, where:
rapidFireQAs.a: Predicted pCO2 = (1.5xHCO3) + 8 +/- 2.

rapidFireQAs.q: - Therefore:
rapidFireQAs.a: First 20 mins: acute respiratory alkalosis (↑ pH, ↔ HCO3- , ↓ CO2). >20 mins: mixed metabolic acidosis-respiratory alkalosis (↓/↔ pH, ↓ HCO3- , ↓ CO2, ↑ anion-gap). I have only ever seen NBMEs assess the latter. Qbank is not the same as NBME/USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: - As discussed earlier, renal failure causes secondary hyperparathyroidism, where we have:
- However, it is also pass-level you know that in renal failure we also have:
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ K+ , ↓ HCO3- , ↓ pH, ↑ anion gap (U in MUDPILES = uremia = renal failure), with Na+ variable. The kidney normally secretes potassium distally in the cortical collecting duct under the action of aldosterone. So if the kidney is impaired, we can’t do that, so K+ is ↑. Likewise, we normally have HCO3- reabsorbed in the PCT and H+ secreted in the cortical collecting duct, so if we can’t do either of those things, blood HCO3- and pH ↓. HY Pulmonary acid/base findings

rapidFireQAs.q: - Acute asthma attack and PE: ↓ pCO2, no change HCO3- , ↑ pH,
rapidFireQAs.a: The key here is that these conditions cause acute respiratory alkalosis, not acidosis, as I mentioned in above table. Students normally this up and think pCO2 is high. pCO2 only goes ↑ if the patient becomes tired as an asthma attack prolongs. But initially, for both of these conditions, we have low pCO2, not high. Bicarb is unchanged because it takes a minimum of 12-24 hours for bicarb excretion to be sufficiently modulated by the kidney. Tangentially, metabolic acid-base disturbances are instantly compensated for by changes in pCO2 by simply breathing more or less.

rapidFireQAs.q: - Patients with COPD and obstructive sleep apnea are chronic CO2 retainers, where we have:
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ pCO2, ↑ HCO3- , ↓ pH. Bicarb goes up to compensate. Miscellaneous HY acid/base

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base role of aldosterone
rapidFireQAs.a: causes direct proton secretion at apical membrane of cortical collecting duct

rapidFireQAs.q: How does aldosterone relate to ENac?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased reabsorption of Na at basolateral membrane means decreased intracellular Na → favorable high-low gradient of Na from urine into tubular cell → ENac upregulates on apical membrane to increase movement of Na into tubular cell

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base / biochemical disturbance in Addison
rapidFireQAs.a: low Na, high K, low bicarb, low pH (metabolic acidosis)

rapidFireQAs.q: Fatigued patient + hyperpigmentation + low BP
rapidFireQAs.a: Addison disease (primary hypoadrenalism; low aldosterone + low cortisol)

rapidFireQAs.q: Infective cause of Addison
rapidFireQAs.a: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (WFS)

rapidFireQAs.q: What is WFS
rapidFireQAs.a: hemorrhagic (not ischemic) necrosis of adrenal glands

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of WFS
rapidFireQAs.a: meningococcal septicemia (non-blanching rash)

rapidFireQAs.q: Low BP in WFS + fluids are given; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: give dexamethasone to compensate for low cortisol

rapidFireQAs.q: If WFS is hemorrhagic necrosis, what HY scenario contrasts
rapidFireQAs.a: Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of anterior pituitary following labor

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of Sheehan
rapidFireQAs.a: anterior pituitary doubles in size during pregnancy to increase prolactin secretion; blood loss during labor → ischemic infarction

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE arrow Q for Sheehan
rapidFireQAs.a: down ACTH, down TSH, down prolactin, up aldosterone (NBME exam)

rapidFireQAs.q: How do you Dx Addison disease
rapidFireQAs.a: ACTH stimulation test (if cortisol doesn’t go up appreciably, Dx confirmed)

rapidFireQAs.q: Weird hematologic finding in Addison
rapidFireQAs.a: eosinophilia (don’t go chasing ova, stool, parasites)

rapidFireQAs.q: Why fatigue in Addison
rapidFireQAs.a: low cortisol causes chronic fatigue syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: Why hyperpigmentation in Addison
rapidFireQAs.a: low cortisol, so less negative feedback at hypothalamus + anterior pituitary → increase in CRH → increase in POMC (precursor to ACTH and alpha-MSH)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Addison
rapidFireQAs.a: fludrocortisone

rapidFireQAs.q: Important point about fludrocortisone
rapidFireQAs.a: corticosteroid with high mineralocorticoid effect (acts like aldosterone) → can be used to overcome low aldosterone + low cortisol caused by Addison

rapidFireQAs.q: Important point about prednisone + hydrocortisone + dexamethasone
rapidFireQAs.a: glucocorticoids with very low mineralocorticoid effect (do not act like aldosterone) → hydrocortisone classically used to treat secondary hypoadrenalism (only decreased cortisol)

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of Addison
rapidFireQAs.a: autoimmune, typically part of polyglandular syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of secondary hypoadrenalism
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased ACTH production → usually due to impingement by pituitary tumor (e.g, prolactinoma); can also be caused by Sheehan syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: ACTH levels in Addison vs secondary hypoadrenalism
rapidFireQAs.a: high in Addison; low in secondary

rapidFireQAs.q: Renin levels in Addison?
rapidFireQAs.a: high

rapidFireQAs.q: Potassium levels in secondary hypoadrenalism?
rapidFireQAs.a: normal because aldosterone intact through RAAS; cause is merely decreased ACTH

rapidFireQAs.q: Primary hyperaldosteronism
rapidFireQAs.a: Conn syndrome (tumor) or diffuse hyperplasia (autoimmune)

rapidFireQAs.q: Renin level in Conn syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: low

rapidFireQAs.q: High BP + high renin/aldosterone ratio in young woman
rapidFireQAs.a: fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD)

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of fibromuscular dysplasia?
rapidFireQAs.a: MR angiography of renal arteries

rapidFireQAs.q: High BP + high renin/aldosterone ratio in older patient with cardiovascular disease
rapidFireQAs.a: renal artery stenosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of renal artery stenosis
rapidFireQAs.a: atherosclerosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with high BP + given ACEi + now creatinine increases; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: renal artery stenosis or FMD

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base / biochemical disturbance in RAS or FMD
rapidFireQAs.a: high Na, low K, high bicarb, high pH (metabolic alkalosis)

rapidFireQAs.q: How does RAAS work?
rapidFireQAs.a: Low blood volume → JGC secrete renin → renin cleaves angiotensinogen (produced by the liver) in the plasma into angiotensin I → AT-I goes to lungs and is cleaved by ACE into AT-II → AT-II goes to zona glomerulosa of adrenal cortex → upregulates aldosterone synthase → converts 11-deoxycorticosterone into aldosterone

rapidFireQAs.q: Important functions of AT-II unrelated to aldosterone?
rapidFireQAs.a: potent vasoconstrictor on systemic arterioles (increases afterload) + renal efferent arterioles (increases filtration fraction [GFR/RPF] in setting of low blood volume, meaning that GFR is maintained despite low renal plasma flow) + increases PCT reabsorption of Na

rapidFireQAs.q: Why is AT-II-mediated PCT reabsorption of Na important?
rapidFireQAs.a: water follows Na; mechanism to increase fluid retention in setting of low blood volume

rapidFireQAs.q: Effect of giving ACEi on efferent arteriolar diameter
rapidFireQAs.a: increases diameter

rapidFireQAs.q: ACEi (e.g., enalapril) effect on RAAS
rapidFireQAs.a: increases renin, increases AT-I, decreases AT-II, decreases aldosterone

rapidFireQAs.q: ARB (e.g., valsartan) effect on RAAS
rapidFireQAs.a: increases renin, increases AT-I, increases AT-II, decreases aldosterone

rapidFireQAs.q: Spironolactone effect on RAAS
rapidFireQAs.a: increases renin, increases AT-I, increases AT-II, increases aldosterone

rapidFireQAs.q: Eplerenone vs spironolactone
rapidFireQAs.a: eplerenone way less likely to cause gynecomastia

rapidFireQAs.q: If suspected Dx of Conn syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: CT abdomen

rapidFireQAs.q: If CT abdomen negative (hyperplasia not tumor)
rapidFireQAs.a: adrenal venous sampling to confirm

rapidFireQAs.q: What is pheochromocytoma
rapidFireQAs.a: catecholamine-secreting tumor of adrenal medulla

rapidFireQAs.q: Paroxysmal headaches/palpitations (high BP) + normal electrolytes
rapidFireQAs.a: pheochromocytoma (PCC)

rapidFireQAs.q: Paroxysmal headaches/palpitations (high BP) + high glucose
rapidFireQAs.a: PCC (catecholamines cause liver to make glucose)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for PCC
rapidFireQAs.a: phenoxybenzamine first (irreversible alpha-1 blocker); never beta-blocker first

rapidFireQAs.q: Why phenoxybenzamine first to treat PCC
rapidFireQAs.a: if you give beta-blocker first, you get “unopposed alpha,” meaning all of the NE + E (catecholamines) floating around bind to alpha-1, causing massive arteriolar vasoconstriction, shooting BP through the roof

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of PCC
rapidFireQAs.a: urinary or serum metanephrines

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets PCC
rapidFireQAs.a: NF1, MEN2A/2B (ret gene)

rapidFireQAs.q: PCC adults or kids?
rapidFireQAs.a: adults

rapidFireQAs.q: PCC-like presentation in kids?
rapidFireQAs.a: neuroblastoma (n-myc gene)

rapidFireQAs.q: Dancing eyes + high BP + midline mass in kid
rapidFireQAs.a: neuroblastoma

rapidFireQAs.q: Dancing eyes? ?
rapidFireQAs.a: opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (seen in neuroblastoma; yes, weird)

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of neuroblastoma
rapidFireQAs.a: abdominal ultrasound

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid with painless flank mass that doesn’t cross midline
rapidFireQAs.a: Wilms tumor

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of Wilms tumor
rapidFireQAs.a: renal ultrasound

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonatal boy with midline suprapubic mass
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior urethral valves

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of posterior urethral valves
rapidFireQAs.a: voiding cystourethrogram

rapidFireQAs.q: Cushing syndrome vs Cushing disease
rapidFireQAs.a: syndrome = what you look like + refers to any cause of Cushingoid appearance; Cushing disease only = anterior pituitary ACTH-secreting tumor; in other words, Cushing disease is a cause of Cushing syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of Cushing syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: exogenous glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone)

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt not on exogenous steroids + Cushingoid; most common cause?
rapidFireQAs.a: Cushing disease most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: Main causes of Cushing syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: exogenous steroids (most common overall), Cushing disease (most common endogenous), small cell bronchogenic carcinoma (ectopic ACTH), cortisol-secreting tumor (or diffuse hyperplasia) of zona fasciculata of adrenal cortex; CRH tumor rare as

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with chronic disease (i.e., IBD, SLE, RA) + Cushingoid; what are the ACTH + cortisol levels
rapidFireQAs.a: need to know this means patient is taking prednisone → low ACTH + low cortisol (prednisone is NOT the same thing as cortisol) → prednisone suppresses CRH and ACTH secretion at hypothalamus and anterior pituitary → decreased endogenous cortisol production

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with Cushing disease; ACTH + cortisol levels?
rapidFireQAs.a: high ACTH + high cortisol

rapidFireQAs.q: Smoker + Cushingoid
rapidFireQAs.a: small cell bronchogenic carcinoma

rapidFireQAs.q: Smoker + Cushingoid; ACTH + cortisol levels?
rapidFireQAs.a: high ACTH (ectopic) + high cortisol

rapidFireQAs.q: When to do dexamethasone suppression test
rapidFireQAs.a: Cushingoid patient not on exogenous glucocorticoids and has high serum cortisol

rapidFireQAs.q: Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
rapidFireQAs.a: tells us yes or no, patient has pathologic cause of Cushing syndrome (i.e., Cushing disease, or SCC of lung, or cortisol-secreting tumor), but we can’t establish the causation from this; if cortisol doesn’t suppress → yes, patient has true Cushing syndrome (proceed to high-dose test); if cortisol suppresses → no, patient does not have Cushing syndrome (do not proceed to high-dose test)

rapidFireQAs.q: High-dose dex
rapidFireQAs.a: only cause of Cushing syndrome that will suppress in response is Cushing disease

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt has no suppression to low-dose dex + suppresses to high-dose
rapidFireQAs.a: Dx = Cushing disease (ACTH secreting tumor of anterior pituitary)

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt has no suppression to low- or high-dose dex
rapidFireQAs.a: ACTH high? → Yes, answer = SCC of lung; No → answer = cortisol-secreting tumor (or diffuse hyperplasia) of adrenal cortex

rapidFireQAs.q: Cushingoid + low ACTH + low cortisol
rapidFireQAs.a: exogenous steroids

rapidFireQAs.q: Cushingoid + low ACTH + high cortisol
rapidFireQAs.a: cortisol-secreting tumor (or diffuse hyperplasia) of adrenal cortex

rapidFireQAs.q: Cushingoid + high ACTH + high cortisol
rapidFireQAs.a: Cushing disease

rapidFireQAs.q: Most accurate test for Dx Cushing syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: 24-hour urine cortisol

rapidFireQAs.q: Why dex test not most accurate?
rapidFireQAs.a: false-positives in e.g., depression, alcoholism

rapidFireQAs.q: Acanthosis nigricans + low K + hyperpigmentation
rapidFireQAs.a: Cushing syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: Why acanthosis nigricans
rapidFireQAs.a: caused by insulin resistance (unrelated: also can be caused by visceral malignancies)

rapidFireQAs.q: Why low K in Cushing syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic elevation of glucocorticoid effect at kidney can push out potassium similar to aldosterone

rapidFireQAs.q: Why hyperpigmentation
rapidFireQAs.a: high ACTH secretion means POMC is high → high alpha-MSH as well

rapidFireQAs.q: Purple striae in obese patient
rapidFireQAs.a: Cushing syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: Why purple striae
rapidFireQAs.a: glucocorticoids weaken collagen → micro bleeding into skin

rapidFireQAs.q: Why hypertension in Cushing syndrome
rapidFireQAs.a: cortisol upregulates alpha-1 receptors on arterioles, thereby allowing NE and E to do their job

rapidFireQAs.q: Graph shows you two scenarios: 1) NE given alone, then BP increases a little; 2) NE + cortisol given together, then BP increases a lot; why the difference?
rapidFireQAs.a: cortisol is permissive of the effects of catecholamines (don’t choose synergistic or additive); once again, cortisol merely allows NE and E to do their job; cortisol isn’t directly increasing BP

rapidFireQAs.q: Why normally ratio of E to NE in the blood is 80/20?
rapidFireQAs.a: NE draining venously out of the adrenal medulla passes through the adrenal cortex → cortisol upregulates PNMT (converts NE to E)

rapidFireQAs.q: What does low cortisol cause?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic fatigue syndrome (as mentioned earlier but super important)

rapidFireQAs.q: Function of PTH
rapidFireQAs.a: increases blood Ca + decreases blood PO4

rapidFireQAs.q: Function of PTH at bone
rapidFireQAs.a: increases bone resorption

rapidFireQAs.q: Cell PTH binds to at bone
rapidFireQAs.a: osteoblast, not -clast

rapidFireQAs.q: If PTH causes bone resorption, why the would it bind to osteoblasts (which build bone)
rapidFireQAs.a: because PTH causes osteoblasts to express RANK-Ligand on their cell surface → binds to RANK receptor on osteoclasts → bone resorption

rapidFireQAs.q: How do osteoclasts resorb bone
rapidFireQAs.a: intracellular carbonic anhydrase II (CAH-II) → creates H2CO3 from H2O and CO2; then the H2CO3 → bicarb + proton → protons accumulate at bone-osteoclast interface → surface for resorption

rapidFireQAs.q: What is teriparatide
rapidFireQAs.a: N-terminus PTH analogue that binds to osteoblasts, and then rather than causing bone resorption, actually stimulates bone growth (difference in mechanism not well elucidated) → used in advanced osteoporosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Avoid teriparatide in whom?
rapidFireQAs.a: Paget disease of bone patients; Hx of osteosarcoma

rapidFireQAs.q: Three effects of PTH at the kidney?
rapidFireQAs.a: 1) it upregulates 1-alpha hydroxylase activity in the PCT (converts inactive 25-OH-D3 into active 1,25-(OH)2-D3; 2) decreases PO4 reabsorption in PCT by downregulating three types of apical membrane brush-border sodium-phosphate symporters; 3) increases Ca reabsorption in the late-DCT by upregulating the apical TRPV5 transporter → reabsorbs calcium.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does secretion in kidney terms mean
rapidFireQAs.a: excretion through the tubular wall (excretion is umbrella term → filtration = excretion through Bowman capsule; secretion = through tubular wall)

rapidFireQAs.q: Primary hyperparathyroidism biochemical disturbance?
rapidFireQAs.a: high Ca, low PO4, high ALP, high PTH

rapidFireQAs.q: Why is ALP high
rapidFireQAs.a: ALP reflects osteoblast activity; if PTH high, then ALP also high (but annoyingly, if PTH is low, ALP will be normal, not low)

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets primary hyperPTH
rapidFireQAs.a: usually parathyroid adenoma (e.g., 22 yr old girl with nodule)

rapidFireQAs.q: Who else gets primaryPTH
rapidFireQAs.a: MEN1 + MEN2A (can be diffuse 4-gland hyperplasia in MEN patients)

rapidFireQAs.q: , what are the MEN syndromes again?
rapidFireQAs.a: Relax. MEN1 = parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas; MEN2A = parathyroid, PCC, medullary thyroid carcinoma; MEN2B = PCC, medullary thyroid carcinoma, mucosal neuromas, and Marfanoid body habitus (“oid” means looks like but ain’t)

rapidFireQAs.q: Question says girl has high Ca + low PO4 + nodule of left, superior parathyroid gland; what’s the embryo derivative?
rapidFireQAs.a: 4th pharyngeal pouch

rapidFireQAs.q: Other weird info I need to know for primaryPTH?
rapidFireQAs.a: Yeah, firstly, urinary Ca is high, not low.

rapidFireQAs.q: , how is that possible if PTH reabsorbs Ca from urine
rapidFireQAs.a: because serum Ca is high, so the net amount in the urine is still high (this is a HY arrow Q that everyone gets wrong); in other words, on the USMLE, in primaryPTH → serum Ca up; serum PO4 down; serum ALP up; urinary Ca up (oh wow)

rapidFireQAs.q: Second weird factoid about primaryPTH
rapidFireQAs.a: urinary cAMP is elevated (USMLE likes this for some magical reason)

rapidFireQAs.q: What is the biochemical disturbance in secondary hyperparathyroidism?
rapidFireQAs.a: Ca and PO4 opposite of primary → low Ca; high PO4, high ALP + high PTH

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets secondaryPTH
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic renal failure

rapidFireQAs.q: Why does chronic renal failure cause secondaryPTH
rapidFireQAs.a: inability to activate vitamin D3 in PCT → decreased Ca absorption through small bowel → low serum Ca → stimulates PTH release; kidney also simply cannot reabsorb Ca as well, further decreasing serum Ca and stimulating PTH release

rapidFireQAs.q: What about low Ca in acute renal failure; doesn’t it take a while for vitamin D effects to occur
rapidFireQAs.a: if low Ca in acute, due to mere inability to reabsorb from urine

rapidFireQAs.q: Why high PO4 in renal disease
rapidFireQAs.a: kidney can’t filter it out; even though there’s less activated D3 and PO4 absorption through small bowel is also decreased, the inability of the kidney to excrete it “wins”

rapidFireQAs.q: Biochemical disturbance of vitamin D deficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: low Ca, low PO4, normal/high PTH, normal/high ALP

rapidFireQAs.q: Function of vitamin D
rapidFireQAs.a: increases Ca + PO4 absorption in the bowel (don’t worry about minimal role in bone)

rapidFireQAs.q: I don’t get it though; if in chronic renal failure there’s vitamin D deficiency due to less activation, why is there low Ca and high PO4? Isn’t vitamin D deficiency always low Ca and low PO4?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic renal failure “wins” in terms of phosphate always → so although low vitamin D, there’s still high PO4.

rapidFireQAs.q: Any changes to the bones in a patient with chronic renal disease
rapidFireQAs.a: renal osteodystrophy

rapidFireQAs.q: Hip fracture in renal failure + x-ray shows “pseudofractures”
rapidFireQAs.a: vitamin D deficiency

rapidFireQAs.q: Osteitis fibrosa cystica
rapidFireQAs.a: high PTH can cause “brown tumors” of bone + cholesterol accumulation in bone

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid with bowing of tibias + chostochondritis + craniotabes
rapidFireQAs.a: rickets (vitamin D deficiency)

rapidFireQAs.q: Adult with pseudofractures
rapidFireQAs.a: osteomalacia (vitamin D deficiency)

rapidFireQAs.q: Where does vitamin D deficiency start
rapidFireQAs.a: stratum basale of skin (asked on USMLE)

rapidFireQAs.q: What is the sequence for production?
rapidFireQAs.a: 7-dehydrocholsterol in skin goes to cholecalciferol via UV-B → then cholecalciferol goes to liver where it takes on a hydroxylation to make 25-hydroxy-D3 (calcidiol) → then this goes to the kidney where, via PTH activing 1-alpha-hydroxylase, it gets converted to active 1,25-(OH)2-D3 → then this goes to small bowel to cause Ca + PO4 absorption

rapidFireQAs.q: If person doesn’t get sunlight, what can he/she not make
rapidFireQAs.a: cholecalciferol (7-dehydro is wrong answer; this is on NBME)

rapidFireQAs.q: What about 7-dehydrocholesterol in relation to sunlight
rapidFireQAs.a: we make this on our own, then UV-B converts it into cholecalciferol

rapidFireQAs.q: Alcoholic who eats plenty of dairy + gets sunlight + has vitamin D deficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased hepatic hydroxylation

rapidFireQAs.q: Inject person with Ca; what happens to their vitamin D notably
rapidFireQAs.a: increased 24,25-(OH)2- D3.
25-OH-D3 is immediately converted to 24,25 as a storage form (think of them as the same)

rapidFireQAs.q: Inject with Ca
rapidFireQAs.a: Ca binds to Ca-sensing receptor at parathyroid gland → negative feedback → causes reduction in PTH release → decreased 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity at kidney → buildup of 25 form → shunted to 24,25 form.

rapidFireQAs.q: Low calcium or potassium in a patient + he/she not responsive to supplementation
rapidFireQAs.a: hypomagnesemia → Mg needed for basal levels of PTH release (so low PTH → low Ca) + renal retention of K

rapidFireQAs.q: Alcoholic + low Ca or low K not responsive to supplementation
rapidFireQAs.a: check serum magnesium

rapidFireQAs.q: Why low Mg in alcoholic
rapidFireQAs.a: dietary deficiency

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets high vitamin D (hypervitaminosis D)
rapidFireQAs.a: granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis) → don’t be the fool who says “girl tried to commit suicide by ODing on vitamin D pills?”

rapidFireQAs.q: Why high vitamin D in sarcoidosis
rapidFireQAs.a: epithelioid (activated) macrophages secrete 1-alpha hydroxylase → activate vitamin D → increased small bowel absorption

rapidFireQAs.q: Ca and PTH levels in sarcoidosis
rapidFireQAs.a: high Ca, low PTH (negative feedback)

rapidFireQAs.q: Sarcoidosis, any weird fact they ask about Ca?
rapidFireQAs.a: “decreased Ca in feces” (makes sense)

rapidFireQAs.q: Biochemical disturbance in high vit D
rapidFireQAs.a: high Ca, normal or high PO4, normal or low PTH, normal or low ALP (USMLE will only give you one correct answer, don’t worry, but I write the possibilities here so you don’t get a Q where you see normal PTH or PO4 and are wondering , but Ca always up)

rapidFireQAs.q: Sarcoidosis other weird info
rapidFireQAs.a: increased serum ACE (correct, angiotensin-converting enzyme; weird)

rapidFireQAs.q: Sarcoidosis, what happens first, high urinary Ca or high serum Ca
rapidFireQAs.a: high urinary Ca (kidney will compensate before serum levels go up)

rapidFireQAs.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR shows nodularity; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: sarcoidosis; nodularity just means “bihilar lymphadenopathy”

rapidFireQAs.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR shows nodularity; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “noncaseating granulomas” (sarcoidosis)

rapidFireQAs.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR is normal Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: asthma (1/3 of asthma patients only have dry cough; this is called cough-variant asthma)

rapidFireQAs.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR is normal Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “increased activation of mast cells” (asthma)

rapidFireQAs.q: Mutation in calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid gland
rapidFireQAs.a: loss of negative feedback → PTH goes up, serum Ca up

rapidFireQAs.q: Mutation in calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid gland
rapidFireQAs.a: cause of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH)

rapidFireQAs.q: High PTH + high serum Ca + low urinary Ca
rapidFireQAs.a: FHH

rapidFireQAs.q: High PTH + high serum Ca + high urinary Ca
rapidFireQAs.a: primary PTH

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for low urinary Ca in FHH?
rapidFireQAs.a: not fully elucidated, but literature suggests increased tubular reabsorption, possibly paracellular, as serum Mg in FHH elevated relative to primaryPTH

rapidFireQAs.q: What is cinacalcet
rapidFireQAs.a: calcimimetic → activates Ca-sensing receptor at PTH gland

rapidFireQAs.q: When to use cinacalcet
rapidFireQAs.a: tertiary hyperPTH

rapidFireQAs.q: What is tertiary hyperparathyroidism?
rapidFireQAs.a: classically seen in renal transplant patients; autonomous four-gland hypersecretion of PTH following long-term secondary hyperparathyroidism and hypocalcemia → parathyroid chief cell hyperplasia that does not resolve with renal transplant → result is high Ca, variable PO4 (high if still renal impaired), high ALP, high PTH

rapidFireQAs.q: What is pseudohypoparathyroidism?
rapidFireQAs.a: insensitivity to PTH → high PTH but low Ca + high PO4

rapidFireQAs.q: Anything special about pseudohypoparathyroidism?
rapidFireQAs.a: Yes. This is one of the highest yield yet underemphasized conditions on the USMLE Step 1. In other words, my students get these Qs on the exam regularly but the resources don’t emphasize the different types of this condition

rapidFireQAs.q: What is presentation of pseudohypoparathyroidism?
rapidFireQAs.a: need to know Types 1a, 1b, 2

rapidFireQAs.q: Type 1a = Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy = is simply the name of the phenotype
rapidFireQAs.a: AHO has shortened 4th + 5th metacarpals, short stature + intellectual disability + urinary cAMP does not increase with exogenous PTH administration (normally should go up in response to PTH)

rapidFireQAs.q: Type 1b
rapidFireQAs.a: high PTH + low Ca + high PO4 + no AHO phenotype (just biochemical disturbance)

rapidFireQAs.q: Type 2
rapidFireQAs.a: same as Type 1b but urinary cAMP increases in response to exogenous PTH

rapidFireQAs.q: Mike, this sounds pedantic though. The USMLE really asks about pseudohypoparathyroidism like that?
rapidFireQAs.a: Yeah. They ask it as arrow questions. And I personally had two pseudohypoPTH Qs on my Step 1 + my students do.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism?
rapidFireQAs.a: AHO phenotype but no biochemical disturbance

rapidFireQAs.q: Graves disease parameters
rapidFireQAs.a: low TSH, high T3, high T4, increased iodine uptake

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of Graves
rapidFireQAs.a: activating TSH-receptor antibody, called TSI – thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for Graves
rapidFireQAs.a: propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole to address thyroid derangement

rapidFireQAs.q: PTU and methimazole MOAs
rapidFireQAs.a: both inhibit thyroperoxidase, but PTU also inhibits peripheral conversion by inhibiting 5-deiodinase → propylthiouracil is a longer word than methimazole, so it’s the one that does both

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for tachycardia in Graves
rapidFireQAs.a: propranolol (because beta-blockade also decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3)

rapidFireQAs.q: Important point about Graves?
rapidFireQAs.a: proptosis/exophthalmos + pretibial myxedema are specific; in other words, there are numerous causes of hyperthyroidism (e.g., toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, etc.), but only Graves will cause the eye findings

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for ophthalmopathy in Graves
rapidFireQAs.a: steroids

rapidFireQAs.q: Why do the eye findings occur in Graves?
rapidFireQAs.a: glycosaminoglycan deposition in/around extra-ocular muscles

rapidFireQAs.q: High BP + fever + increased CK
rapidFireQAs.a: thyroid storm (Tx with PTU + propranolol)

rapidFireQAs.q: What is the role of potassium iodide (KI) in hyperthyroid Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: shuts off gland production (Wolff- Chaikoff effect) → answer in person exposed to nuclear fallout or radioiodine vapors in laboratory

rapidFireQAs.q: Hashimoto parameters
rapidFireQAs.a: high TSH, low T3, low T4, decreased iodine uptake

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism for Hashimoto
rapidFireQAs.a: antibodies against thyroperoxidase + thyroglobulin; anti-microsomal

rapidFireQAs.q: Histo of Hashimoto
rapidFireQAs.a: lymphocytic infiltrate (easy to remember bc the non-eponymous name for Hashimoto is chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis)

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + low mood + BMI 26
rapidFireQAs.a: Hashimoto

rapidFireQAs.q: Proximal muscle weakness in Hashimoto + increased serum CK
rapidFireQAs.a: hypothyroid myopathy

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + decreased ability to get up from chair unassisted + HR of 60
rapidFireQAs.a: Hashimoto

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + high cholesterol + high hepatic AST + HR of 55
rapidFireQAs.a: Hashimoto (hypothyroidism can cause bradycardia, high cholesterol, and high AST [the latter is weird, correct])

rapidFireQAs.q: Thyroid cancer in Hashimoto
rapidFireQAs.a: thyroid lymphoma (autoimmune diseases → increased risk of lymphoma)

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + viral infection + very tender thyroid
rapidFireQAs.a: subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain)

rapidFireQAs.q: De Quervain parameters
rapidFireQAs.a: triphasic → causes hyper-, then hypo-, then rebounds to euthyroid state → most important point is that iodine uptake is DECREASED in de Quervain + drug-induced thyroiditis, even if patient is in a hyper-phase.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for de Quervain thyroiditis?
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAIDs

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + very tender thyroid + HR of 88 + tremulousness + heat intolerance
rapidFireQAs.a: low TSH, high T3, high T4, decreased iodine uptake (in contrast to Graves, which is painless and uptake is high)

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + gave birth to healthy boy 6 months ago following uncomplicated labor + no weight change or mood disturbance + on no meds + vitals WNL + dry skin + thyroid gland enlarged and non-tender + TSH high + T4 low; most likely explanation for these findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: “thyroiditis” → Dx = postpartum thyroiditis (a type of silent thyroiditis) → characterized by thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism (1/3 of women experience both phases; 1/3 experience just hyperthyroid phase; 1/3 only hypothyroid phase); affects 5-10% of women postpartum; hyperthyroid phase usually occurs 1-4 months postpartum; hypothyroid phase occurs about 4-8 months postpartum; thought to be caused by postpartum immunologic rebound (immune system normally suppressed during pregnancy); Dx w/ Hx + ordering serum TSH; increased risk of progression to Hashimoto; Tx w/ short course of propranolol if hyperthyroid; give short course of levothyroxine if hypothyroid

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for subacute thyroiditis
rapidFireQAs.a: aspirin first, not steroids; steroids may be used later

rapidFireQAs.q: Drugs causing thyroiditis
rapidFireQAs.a: lithium + amiodarone

rapidFireQAs.q: Surreptitious thyrotoxicosis
rapidFireQAs.a: self- injection of thyroxine → low TSH, high T3, high T4, small thyroid gland with decreased uptake

rapidFireQAs.q: Injection of triiodothyroinine (T3)
rapidFireQAs.a: TSH will go down, T3 goes up (clearly), T4 does not go up because T3 isn’t converted to T4; only T4 is converted to T3

rapidFireQAs.q: Injection of thyroxine
rapidFireQAs.a: TSH will go down (negative feedback), T4 goes up (clearly), T3 goes up (due to peripheral conversion), reverse T3 also goes up

rapidFireQAs.q: What is reverse T3?
rapidFireQAs.a: an inactive form of T3; T4 is converted peripherally into T3 (active) and reverse T3 (inactive)

rapidFireQAs.q: Anything else I need to know about reverse T3?
rapidFireQAs.a: it’s increased in euthyroid sick syndrome → times of stress/surgery/illness → cortisol increases → cortisol decreases conversion of T4 to active T3, so more T4 is converted to reverse T3 → parameters in euthyroid sick syndrome: normal TSH, normal T4, low T3, high reverse T3

rapidFireQAs.q: What is sublinical hypothyroidism
rapidFireQAs.a: high TSH but normal T3 + T4 (don’t confuse with ESS)

rapidFireQAs.q: Want to check thyroid function, what’s the first thing to order
rapidFireQAs.a: TSH

rapidFireQAs.q: Want to check thyroid function in pregnancy, what’s the first thing to order
rapidFireQAs.a: free-T4

rapidFireQAs.q: What is free-T4
rapidFireQAs.a: most thyroid hormone is protein-bound and inactive; free-T4 tells you definitively whether the patient has thyroid derangement or not

rapidFireQAs.q: Pregnancy and thyroid
rapidFireQAs.a: estrogen causes increased thyroid-binding globulin production by the liver → mops of T4 → less free-T4 → less negative feedback at hypothalamus + anterior pituitary → TSH goes up transiently to compensate → more T4 made → free-T4 rebounds to normal but now total T4 is high → parameters you need to know for pregnancy: normal TSH + high total T4 + normal free-T4 + normal free T3 + high thyroid-binding globulin

rapidFireQAs.q: Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy
rapidFireQAs.a: LH, FSH, TSH, hCG all share same alpha-subunit; their beta-subunits differ; some women have increases sensitivity of TSH receptor to alpha-subunit, so high hCG in early pregnancy can stimulate thyroid gland and cause transient hyperthyroidism

rapidFireQAs.q: Hashimoto in pregnancy
rapidFireQAs.a: increase pregnant woman’s dose of levothyroxine by 50%

rapidFireQAs.q: Graves in pregnancy
rapidFireQAs.a: avoid methimazole in first trimester (teratogenic; causes aplasia cutis congenita) → give PTU in first-trimester → in second + third trimesters, switch from PTU to methimazole (methimazole no longer teratogenic later in pregnancy + PTU is heavily hepatotoxic)

rapidFireQAs.q: Pt being treated for Graves + mouth ulcers
rapidFireQAs.a: agranulocytosis (neutropenia) caused by methimazole or PTU.

rapidFireQAs.q: Young child with normal free-T4 and low total T4
rapidFireQAs.a: thyroid-binding globulin deficiency (opposite of pregnancy)

rapidFireQAs.q: Young child + large belly + large tongue + hypotonia
rapidFireQAs.a: cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism)

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of cretinism
rapidFireQAs.a: iodine deficiency

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of hyperthyroidism in elderly
rapidFireQAs.a: toxic multinodular goiter

rapidFireQAs.q: Evaluation of thyroid cancer, first step?
rapidFireQAs.a: palpation of thyroid gland

rapidFireQAs.q: If thyroid nodule present, then check TSH; if TSH normal or high
rapidFireQAs.a: ultrasound first, then FNA; if TSH low, do radioiodine uptake scan; thyroid cancer is cold, not hot, which is why no ultimate FNA with low TSH

rapidFireQAs.q: Struma ovarii
rapidFireQAs.a: thyroid hormone secreting ovarian germ cell tumor

rapidFireQAs.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis parameters
rapidFireQAs.a: low serum Na, high serum K (hyperkalemia), low total body K, low bicarb, low pH, low CO2 (all exceedingly HY)

rapidFireQAs.q: Why low serum Na in DKA
rapidFireQAs.a: osmotic effect of high glucose in blood → dilutional hyponatremia; in addition, there’s believed to be a contributory renal mechanism related to increased absorption of water in the PCT due to increased SGLT2 reabsorption of glucose in PCT

rapidFireQAs.q: Then what does low total body potassium mean
rapidFireQAs.a: just to be clear, the patient is hyperkalemic (high K in the blood) yet has low K overall in the body → kidney senses high K in urine and therefore increases excretion of it (kaliuresis) → body is now losing K → but three above mechanisms leading to hyperkalemia continue unabated, so K stays high in serum even though body is now urinating it out.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why does the potassium stuff matter so much with DKA
rapidFireQAs.a: because when you Tx DKA and start giving insulin (fluids first btw; giving insulin immediately is the wrong answer; give insulin after first administering a bolus of normal saline), K will now be driven into the cells, which will bring K down to normal in the serum, but bear in mind it was low in the cells → so now risk of normal in cells but low in blood → need to supplement K to patient when K falls below 5.2 (normal is 3.5-5 mEq/L). Stop all insulin if K falls below 3.3.

rapidFireQAs.q: Overweight, middle-age patient with polydipsia + polyuria
rapidFireQAs.a: type II DM

rapidFireQAs.q: High in serum in type II DM
rapidFireQAs.a: insulin is high initially; ketones absent (only ketones in DKA; DKA is type I only)

rapidFireQAs.q: Type II diabetic crisis?
rapidFireQAs.a: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic non-ketotic syndrome (HHNS) → still give fluids first

rapidFireQAs.q: Glucose numbers in DKA vs HHNS
rapidFireQAs.a: low-hundreds for DKA (i.e., 2-300s); can be 600-1000 for HHNS

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in aspirin toxicity first 20 mins
rapidFireQAs.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, normal O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in aspirin toxicity after 20 mins
rapidFireQAs.a: mixed metabolic acidosis-respiratory alkalosis (low CO2, low pH, normal O2, low bicarb)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for aspirin toxicity
rapidFireQAs.a: bicarb (increased excretion through urinary alkalinization)

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in PE
rapidFireQAs.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, low O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in asthma
rapidFireQAs.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, low O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

rapidFireQAs.q: Electrolyte abnormality in anorexia
rapidFireQAs.a: hypokalemia

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of death in anorexia
rapidFireQAs.a: arrhythmia from hypokalemia

rapidFireQAs.q: Refeeding syndrome (even if normal BMI)
rapidFireQAs.a: hypophosphatemia

rapidFireQAs.q: Amenorrhea in anorexia
rapidFireQAs.a: low FSH + low estrogen (hypogonadotropic)

rapidFireQAs.q: Premature ovarian failure + Turner syndrome + menopause
rapidFireQAs.a: high FSH (low inhibin) + low estrogen

rapidFireQAs.q: High BMI female + irregular menstrual cycles
rapidFireQAs.a: anovulation

rapidFireQAs.q: Anovulation + hirsutism
rapidFireQAs.a: PCOS

rapidFireQAs.q: Anovulation. Cause USMLE wants?
rapidFireQAs.a: insulin resistance → causes abnormal GnRH pulsation

rapidFireQAs.q: Why hirsutism in anovulation
rapidFireQAs.a: abnormal GnRH pulsation causes high LH/FSH ratio

rapidFireQAs.q: Why high LH/FSH ratio important in anovulation/PCOS
rapidFireQAs.a: ovulation stimulated when follicle not ready → no ovulation (anovulation) → follicle retained as cyst

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s LH do?
rapidFireQAs.a: Stimulates theca interna cells (females) and Leydig cells (males) to make androgens

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s FSH do?
rapidFireQAs.a: Stimulates granulosa cells (females) and Sertoli cells (males) to make aromatase; also primes follicles

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for PCOS
rapidFireQAs.a: if high BMI, weight loss first always on USMLE

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for PCOS if they ask for meds and/or weight loss already tried
rapidFireQAs.a: OCPs (if not wanting pregnancy); clomiphene (if wanting pregnancy)

rapidFireQAs.q: PCOS increases risk of what
rapidFireQAs.a: endometrial cancer (unopposed estrogen)

rapidFireQAs.q: Where does ADH (vasopressin) act
rapidFireQAs.a: medullary collecting duct → causes aquaporin insertion on apical membrane → enables free H2O reabsorption

rapidFireQAs.q: Where is ADH made?
rapidFireQAs.a: supraoptic nucleus of hypothalamus → merely stored in posterior pituitary

rapidFireQAs.q: Where is oxytocin made
rapidFireQAs.a: paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus → merely stored in p. pituitary.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neurophysins I’ve heard about. What are those
rapidFireQAs.a: Showed up in UWorld → carrier proteins needed to transport oxytocin + ADH from hypothalamus to posterior pituitary

rapidFireQAs.q: When does ADH go up
rapidFireQAs.a: when serum sodium too high → brings sodium back down; ADH will also be secreted in response to lower blood volume, although aldosterone is major volume regulator; ADH is main tonicity regulator

rapidFireQAs.q: When considering SIADH vs diabetes insipidus (DI) vs psychogenic polydipsia (PP)
rapidFireQAs.a: what’s the next best step in evaluation/management → fluid restriction

rapidFireQAs.q: SIADH important causes
rapidFireQAs.a: small cell bronchogenic carcinoma ectopic ACTH, or head trauma (can actually cause SIADH or DI)

rapidFireQAs.q: SIADH parameters
rapidFireQAs.a: high urine osmolality (concentrated) + low serum sodium (normal is 135-145)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for SIADH
rapidFireQAs.a: if small cell lung cancer, chemotherapy (HY to know you can’t do surgery for small cell); if insufficient, give -vaptans (conivaptan, tolvaptan), which are ADH receptor antagonists, or demeclocycline (a tetracycline antibiotic that causes nephrogenic DI, but is a Tx for SIADH).

rapidFireQAs.q: Central diabetes insipidus
rapidFireQAs.a: lack of production by hypothalamus or storage problem of posterior pituitary → low ADH + low urine osmolality (dilute urine) + high serum sodium (concentrated serum)

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of CDI
rapidFireQAs.a: idiopathic, local malignancy, or head trauma

rapidFireQAs.q: Nephrogenic DI
rapidFireQAs.a: lack of sensitivity of kidney V2 receptors to ADH → high ADH, low urine osmolality (dilute urine) + high serum sodium (concentrated serum)

rapidFireQAs.q: Cause of NDI
rapidFireQAs.a: lithium, demeclocycline

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with bipolar disorder + tremors + polyuria + polydipsia
rapidFireQAs.a: NDI

rapidFireQAs.q: Dude jumps into cold lake; what happens to central blood volume + atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) + ADH levels?
rapidFireQAs.a: CBV up (cold → sympathetic activation → alpha-1 agonism peripherally to decrease surface area of blood vessels to conserve heat → blood forced to core) + ANP up (if CBV up, then right atrial stretch up; ANP is body’s natural diuretic → causes PCT to decrease Na reabsorption) + ADH down (baroreceptor at carotid sinus senses greater stretch → has a role not just on HR but also ADH release)

rapidFireQAs.q: Psychogenic polydipsia (PP)?
rapidFireQAs.a: person drinks too much → low serum sodium + low urine osmolality

rapidFireQAs.q: Prolactin does what
rapidFireQAs.a: milk production → acts through JAK/STAT tyrosine kinase

rapidFireQAs.q: Oxytocin does what
rapidFireQAs.a: milk letdown/secretion

rapidFireQAs.q: Growth hormone in young
rapidFireQAs.a: giantism; in adults → acromegaly

rapidFireQAs.q: Important points about acromegaly
rapidFireQAs.a: causes diabetes mellitus (GH causes insulin resistance), hypertension, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthritis, cardiomyopathy; and yes, prognathism (lantern jaw)

rapidFireQAs.q: Growth hormone acts directly at tissues?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants you to know it causes liver to increase insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which acts peripherally

rapidFireQAs.q: Which hormone counteracts GH
rapidFireQAs.a: somatostatin → generally acts to shut off other hormone secretions, and antagonizes the effects of GH (can be Tx for acromegaly)

rapidFireQAs.q: What is pegvisomant?
rapidFireQAs.a: GH receptor antagonist

rapidFireQAs.q: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)
rapidFireQAs.a: caused by 21, 11, or 17 hydroxylase deficiency in adrenal cortex (21 is 90-95% of cases) → autosomal recessive conditions

rapidFireQAs.q: 21 hydroxylase deficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: severe lack of mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid production by adrenal → low BP + high K + high DHEA-S (adrenal androgen)

rapidFireQAs.q: 11 hydroxylase deficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: adrenal can still make 11-deoxycorticosterone in zona glomerulosa + 11- deoxycortisol in zona fasciculata → BP not low (sometimes high) + K not high; DHEA-S still high

rapidFireQAs.q: 17 hydroxylase deficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: can’t convert pregnenolone + progesterone to 17-OH forms → adrenal gland makes aldosterone in excess but not cortisol or DHEA-S

rapidFireQAs.q: What does ACTH do at adrenal gland
rapidFireQAs.a: upregulates desmolase, which converts cholesterol into pregnenolone to start adrenal hormone synthesis

rapidFireQAs.q: What does angiotensin II do at the adrenal gland
rapidFireQAs.a: upregulates aldosterone synthase, converting 11- deoxycorticosterone into aldosterone

rapidFireQAs.q: What is metyrapone testing?
rapidFireQAs.a: 11-beta hydroxylase inhibitor → can be used in the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency or Cushing → re the former, if you give metyrapone, cortisol should go down normally and ACTH + 11-deoxycorticosterone should go up; if ACTH goes up but 11- deoxycorticosterone doesn’t → adrenal dysfunction (Addison); if ACTH doesn’t go up, then it’s secondary hypoadrenalism) HY ENDOCRINE

rapidFireQAs.q: Normal calcium
Tx of hypercalcemia
rapidFireQAs.a: 10.2-12 → normal saline (0.9% NaCl)

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of hypercalcemia
rapidFireQAs.a: 12-14 → normal saline (0.9% NaCl) only if asymptomatic; add bisphosphonate (e.g., pamidronate) if symptomatic

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of hypercalcemia
rapidFireQAs.a: 14+ → normal saline (0.9% NaCl) + bisphosphonate

rapidFireQAs.q: Low calcium or potassium in alcoholic
rapidFireQAs.a: hypomagnesemia is cause

rapidFireQAs.q: Back pain in elderly patient with hypercalcemia
rapidFireQAs.a: multiple myeloma or metastases

rapidFireQAs.q: Polycythemia + hypercalcemia + smoker + red urine
rapidFireQAs.a: RCC (paraneoplasic EPO + PTH-rp)

rapidFireQAs.q: Electrolyte disturbance in sarcoid
rapidFireQAs.a: hypercalcemia → LOW PTH + high calcium

rapidFireQAs.q: Hypercalcemia in sarcoid, why?
rapidFireQAs.a: epithelioid (activated) macrophages produce 1-alpha hydroxylase, thereby activating vitamin D3

rapidFireQAs.q: Two main causes of pseudogout
rapidFireQAs.a: primary hyperparathyroidism + hemochromatosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Two ways pseudogout presents
rapidFireQAs.a: monoarthritis of large joint (i.e., knee) or osteoarthritis-like presentation in someone with primary hyperparathyroidism or hemochromatosis

rapidFireQAs.q: PTU and methimazole are used for what?
rapidFireQAs.a: Tx of Graves

rapidFireQAs.q: 17F + 1-year Hx of autoimmune thyroiditis + 2-year Hx of type I DM + Candidal infections since childhood; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis → two points: 1) clearly the Candidal infections can’t be due to the diabetes if she’s had them since childhood and only DM for two years; 2) USMLE likes “autoimmune conditions go together,” the same way it likes “autoimmune conditions and immunodeficiencies go together”; in other words, CMC and IgA deficiency are examples of immunodeficiencies with an autoimmune origin, so the vignette mentioning autoimmune phenomenon isn’t an accident.

rapidFireQAs.q: Thyroid dysfunction on ventilator
rapidFireQAs.a: euthyroid sick syndrome → normal TSH, normal T4, low T3, high reverse T3 (cortisol decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, allowing more to go to reverse T3)

rapidFireQAs.q: is reverse T3?
rapidFireQAs.a: an inactive form of T3; all you need to know is that if T4 goes up (e.g., in Graves), reverse T3 should be up because T4 will convert to both T3 and reverse T3; it is also elevated in euthyroid sick syndrome (and T3 down!)

rapidFireQAs.q: Familial thyroid cancer
rapidFireQAs.a: medullary (even if they mention nothing else related to MEN 2A/2B); apple- green birefringence on Congo red stain due to amyloid deposition; serum calcitonin high

rapidFireQAs.q: Calcitonin mechanism of action
rapidFireQAs.a: inhibits osteoclast activity (not the opposite of PTH; in other words, doesn’t put calcium back into bone; it merely caps the Ca that can resorb out of the bone)

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common thyroid cancer
rapidFireQAs.a: papillary; extends lymphatogenously; has papillary structure and psammoma bodies on LM; don’t worry about buzzywordy things like Orphan Annie nuclei

rapidFireQAs.q: Follicular carcinoma
rapidFireQAs.a: literally just thyroid follicles on biopsy; will be a cold nodule, like any other type of thyroid cancer (for instance, if you see follicles but it’s a hot nodule w/ increased uptake, that’s a toxic adenoma, rather than follicular thyroid cancer); spreads hematogenously

rapidFireQAs.q: Hashimoto + thyroid cancer + no other histo description
rapidFireQAs.a: thyroid lymphoma → autoimmune diseases increase the risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

rapidFireQAs.q: MEN1
rapidFireQAs.a: pituitary, pancreas, parathyroid (MEN1 gene; chromosome 11)

rapidFireQAs.q: MEN2A
rapidFireQAs.a: parathyroid, medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma

rapidFireQAs.q: MEN2B
rapidFireQAs.a: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, Marfanoid body habitus (“oid” means looks like but ain’t)

rapidFireQAs.q: Riedel thyroiditis
rapidFireQAs.a: fibrosis of thyroid → can extend into adjacent structures, e.g., the esophagus, and resemble anaplastic carcinoma

rapidFireQAs.q: First drug to start in T2DM
rapidFireQAs.a: metformin

rapidFireQAs.q: Side-effect of metformin
rapidFireQAs.a: lactic acidosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Black widow spider bite
rapidFireQAs.a: causes hypocalcemia → give IV calcium gluconate

rapidFireQAs.q: Adult male is 4 feet tall + head and trunk proportional to limbs; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Laron dwarfism (growth hormone receptor defect → insensitivity to GH).

rapidFireQAs.q: Biochemical disturbance in Addison?
rapidFireQAs.a: Low Na, high K, low pH, low bicarb

rapidFireQAs.q: Biochemical disturbance in Conn syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: High Na, low K, high pH, high bicarb

rapidFireQAs.q: 2-year-old boy has cardiac myxoma (correct, not rhabdomyoma) + perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the mouth/lips) + hyperthyroidism; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Carney complex → this is asked on the USMLE → classically triad of cardiac myxoma + perioral melanosis + endocrine hypersecretion (classically bilateral pigmented zona fasciculata hyperplasia resulting Cushing syndrome, but can be hyperthyroidism or growth hormone).

rapidFireQAs.q: Biochemical disturbance in DKA
rapidFireQAs.a: low Na, high serum K (hyperkalemia), low total body K, low bicarb, low pH, low CO2.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + experiment glucose injected IV in two different scenarios: 1) when food is simultaneously consumed orally, and 2) when no food is simultaneously consumed; experiment shows that glucose is cleared faster from circulation when food is concurrently consumed orally; Q asks, which hormone is responsible for these findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP); secreted in response to oral consumption of macronutrients (i.e., carbs, fats, protein); causes insulin secretion; in other words, insulin goes up more when food is consumed orally vs merely received parenterally → faster clearance of plasma glucose.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + receives 50g of glucose IV vs 50g of glucose orally; insulin goes up more when glucose consumed orally; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide → greater insulin secretion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30M + shooting groin pain + increased blood pressure + mother had surgery for thyroid cancer; what’s most likely to establish the cause of the patient’s HTN?
rapidFireQAs.a: urinary metanephrines; diagnosis is MEN 2A → pheochromocytoma + medullary thyroid carcinoma + primary hyperparathyroidism; Tx pheo with phenoxybenzamine (irreversible alpha blocker); shooting groin pain is urolithiasis secondary to hypercalcemia; medullary thyroid cancer causes increased serum calcitonin. For quick comparison, MEN I → pancreatic tumor, pituitary tumor, primary hyperparathyroidism; MEN 2B → pheochromocytoma + medullary thyroid carcinoma + mucosal neuromas + Marfanoid body habitus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 2F + missing superior left parathyroid gland; what’s the embryologic defect?
rapidFireQAs.a: fourth pharyngeal pouch; fourth pouch = superior parathyroids; third pouch = thymus + inferior parathyroids; easiest student -up = selecting arch instead of pouch; pouches = endoderm; arches = mesoderm; clefts/grooves = ectoderm; DiGeorge syndrome → aplasia of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, leading to hypocalcemia, T cell deficiency with absent thymic shadow, cleft lip/palate, and heart defects (tetralogy of Fallot; truncus arteriosus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 26F + hyperpigmentation + BP of 100/60 + muscle weakness; what combination of sodium, potassium, and cortisol are expected in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ sodium, ↑ potassium, ↓ cortisol; Dx is Addison disease; Na is ↓ and K ↑ because aldosterone is ↓. Condition is often caused by antibodies against 21-hydroxylase, which is needed to synthesize both aldosterone and cortisol in the adrenal cortex.

rapidFireQAs.q: Drug is given that increases insulin release; what is the MOA of this drug?
rapidFireQAs.a: increases the ATP/ADP ratio; theoretically, many answers could make sense here; the point is: does the student know the mechanism for insulin release: ATP closes a K+ channel on the beta-islet cells → K+ builds up within the cell → depolarization → Ca2+ then influxes → causes release of insulin-containing vesicles from beta cell; in other words, if a drug increases the ATP/ADP ratio within the beta islet cell, then theoretically that would facilitate insulin release. In real life, sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide) function to close the ATP-gated K+ channel without the need for ATP.

rapidFireQAs.q: 35F + menorrhagia + deep/hoarse voice + delayed tendon reflexes + large, globular heart with crackles at lung bases + low Hct + low MCV; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: check serum TSH; patient likely has Hashimoto (hypothyroidism); can cause menorrhagia, reduced reflexes, and cardiomyopathy. Anemia in this case is likely IDA due to heavy periods (although anemia of chronic disease does indeed present with low MCV on many NBME Qs); other HY findings for hypothyroidism are hypothyroid myopathy (↑ serum CK), ↑ LDL cholesterol, ↑ hepatic transaminases, and low mood; findings such as constipation, cold intolerance, brittle hair, and doughy skin are often omitted from Qs because they’re too easy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + history of alcoholism + serum potassium of 3.2; following K+ administration, potassium remains at 3.2; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypomagnesemia; low Ca2+ and K+ non-responsive to supplementation → answer = check serum magnesium; Mg2+ required for basal level PTH secretion (↓ Mg → ↓ Ca); Mg2+ also inhibits a K+ secretory pump in the distal kidney (↓ Mg → ↑ K wasting); alcoholics are classic group at risk of hypomagnesemia due to mere dietary deficiency (EtOH is 7kcal/g, so they fill up on alcohol).

rapidFireQAs.q: 20F + insulinoma; Q asks about C-peptide, insulin, and serum ketone levels; answer = ↑ C-peptide, insulin, ↓ ketones. C-peptide is a cleavage protein during the production of endogenous insulin, so if endogenous insulin is produced (i.e., via insulinoma), then C-peptide should be proportionally high. Ketogenesis is inhibited by insulin, so ketones must be low. Ketone production requires fatty acid breakdown into acetyl-CoAs as the starting blocks; beta-oxidation is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, which is an intermediate in fatty acid synthesis, as stimulated by insulin.
rapidFireQAs.a: A tangential HY point is that DKA is not seen in type II diabetes because insulin is high initially; DKA is only seen in type I, since insulin is deficient. If a USMLE Q gives you acute type II diabetes and asks what’s high in the patient’s serum, the wrong answer is ketones; the correct answer is insulin (hyperinsulinemia due to insulin resistance).

rapidFireQAs.q: 38M + no proteinuria + LDL 95 mg/dL + BP 120/80 + HbA1c of 10%; Q asks what is most likely to decrease morbidity in this patient? → answer = commence metformin; patient clearly has diabetes with an HbA1c >7s.
rapidFireQAs.a: Diagnosis of diabetes is any of the following: HbA1c >6.5%; two fasting glucose measurements 126 mg/dL or greater; any one random glucose 200 mg/dL or greater. Patients can have normal glucose levels but high HbA1c and therefore be diabetic. It’s to my observation on NBMEs that if the Q wants glycemic control (e.g., “commence metformin”) as the answer, they will give HbA1c as >9%, even though technically any elevation in HbA1c could warrant its commencement. The USMLE Q will often give HbA1c in the 7s as tolerable in a diabetic, where they will make the focus of the Q something else, e.g., LDL >100 (answer = statin) or proteinuria (answer = lisinopril).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + abdo pain an hour after meals + no other PMHx; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: duodenal ulcer due to H. pylori; can also be gastrinoma. If they give you no information apart from duodenal ulcer presentation, H. pylori is answer. Gastrinoma is patient who has recurrent duodenal ulcers despite H. pylori Tx. Gastrinoma can also be part of MEN 1.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + exophthalmos + tachycardia + diarrhea; Dx + risk factor for GIT symptoms?
rapidFireQAs.a: “motility disorder” due to hyperthyroid state (in this case, Graves); “motility disorder” is also answer for hypothyroidism causing constipation, as well as for the diabetes conditions above.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + alcoholic + low calcium; following administration of calcium, serum levels do not rise appreciably; what is risk factor/cause
rapidFireQAs.a: alcoholism causing hypomagnesemia; latter can cause hypocalcemia and/or hypokalemia refractory to supplementation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 27F + gave birth 4 weeks ago + non-tender thyroid + hypothyroid state; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: post- partum thyroiditis; risk factor is recent pregnancy (makes sense).
